Microcontrollers: ESP32 & ARM

Chapter 3 ended with a smart object's "processing" step waved at, but not opened up. This chapter opens it: what's actually inside the chip that reads a sensor and drives an actuator, why the ESP32 specifically became the default IoT board, and why the ARM chip family splits cleanly into two designs built for opposite jobs.

Chapter title: ESP32 & ARM deep dive

Embedded systems

An embedded system is a specialized computer built to do one dedicated job efficiently — unlike the general-purpose computer you're probably reading this on, which is built to do any job reasonably well. Six characteristics define the category: a dedicated function, real-time processing, low power consumption, high reliability, compact size, and cost-effectiveness. Every board in this chapter, and every microcontroller in the smart objects of Chapter 3, is an embedded system by this definition.

An embedded system has two halves: embedded hardware (built around microprocessors and microcontrollers) and embedded software that runs on it. The diagram spells out the pieces that surround the microcontroller at the center: a sensor feeds it real-world data through an A-D converter (analog-to-digital, since sensors usually produce analog voltages but the microcontroller only understands digital numbers); an RTOS (Real-Time Operating System) may schedule its tasks; ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) may handle specialized jobs; and a D-A converter (digital-to-analog) lets it drive an actuator that needs an analog signal rather than a digital one.

Why both converters exist This is the sensor/actuator boundary from Chapter 3, made electrically precise. The physical world is analog (temperature doesn't jump between discrete values), but a microcontroller's logic is entirely digital (1s and 0s). The A-D converter is the doorway data takes coming in from a sensor; the D-A converter is the doorway a signal takes going out to an actuator that expects an analog voltage (like an old-style motor speed controller). Not every actuator needs one — an LED can often be driven directly with a digital HIGH/LOW — but wherever the physical action needs to vary smoothly, a D-A converter (or its cheaper cousin, PWM, covered in Chapter 5) is what makes that possible.

What is a microcontroller?

A Microcontroller (MCU) is a compact integrated circuit containing everything needed to control an embedded system on a single chip — the CPU, memory, and I/O all live on one piece of silicon, unlike a desktop computer where the CPU, RAM, and peripherals are separate components on a motherboard. Five families are named as examples: ESP32, STM32, AVR ATmega328P (the chip actually inside the Arduino Uno from Chapter 3), PIC, and MSP430. The rest of this chapter goes deep on the first of these — the ESP32 — because it's the board this course's labs are built around.

The ESP32

The ESP32 is a low-cost, low-power system-on-chip (SoC) microcontroller with Wi-Fi and dual-mode Bluetooth built in, made by Espressif Systems. That last detail is the whole reason this chip matters for IoT: Chapter 3's Arduino Uno needed an external module bolted on to get wireless connectivity at all; the ESP32 has it on the same die as the processor. This single fact is why so many of the smart-object examples across this course default to the ESP32 rather than a plain Arduino.

FeatureSpec
ProcessorDual-core Xtensa LX6, up to 240 MHz
WirelessWi-Fi, Bluetooth, and BLE
PeripheralsGPIO, ADC, DAC, PWM, SPI, UART, I²C

InterfacePurposeCommon devices
GPIODigital input/outputLEDs, buttons, relays

The pinout diagram is doing real work — read it, don't skip it Notice how many pins carry two, three, or even five labels stacked on top of each other (e.g. a single physical pin might be ADC1_6, RTC, GPIO34 all at once). This is the answer to a question you'll hit the moment you wire up a real ESP32 project: pins are a scarce, shared resource, and the chip's designers multiplexed several functions onto each physical leg. Choosing which pin to use for a sensor is really choosing which of that pin's several roles you want active — and some pins (marked with a "!" for being shared with flash memory) can't be used as ordinary GPIO at all without breaking the board's ability to boot.

The ESP32 spec box on the pinout diagram fills out the picture from slide 10: 32-bit dual-core Xtensa at up to 240 MHz, Wi-Fi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth 4.2 + BLE, 520 KB SRAM, 448 KB ROM, 34 GPIOs, 4× SPI, 3× UART, 2× I²C, 2× I²S, 12-bit ADC, and Ethernet support.

Power modes

ModeCPUWi-Fi/BTPower drawWake-up speed
ActiveRunningActiveHighestInstant
Modem sleepRunningOffMediumVery fast
Light sleepPausedOff/optionalLowFast
Deep sleepOffOffVery lowModerate
HibernationOffOffLowestSlow (full restart)
This table is Chapter 2's "power & cost constraints" driver made literal and controllable. A battery-powered ESP32 sensor node doesn't have to choose once between "always fast" and "always low-power" — it can sit in Deep Sleep between readings (drawing almost nothing) and wake briefly into Active mode to take a measurement and transmit it, trading wake-up latency for months of extra battery life. This is exactly the kind of duty-cycling that makes a battery-powered smart object practical at all.

The ESP32 family has grown fast

VariantYearProcessorMajor improvement
ESP322016Xtensa LX6 (dual-core)Wi-Fi + Bluetooth
ESP32-S22019Xtensa LX7 (single-core)USB OTG, security
ESP32-S32020Xtensa LX7 (dual-core)AI & machine learning
ESP32-C32020RISC-V (single-core)Low power, security
ESP32-C62022RISC-V (single-core)Wi-Fi 6, Zigbee, Thread
ESP32-H22023RISC-V (single-core)Ultra-low power, Matter

Notice the underlying processor architecture itself changes partway through this table — from Xtensa to RISC-V. That's not a minor detail: it means later ESP32 variants aren't just faster versions of the original, they're built on a different instruction set entirely, chosen because RISC-V's open, simpler design suits the newer variants' low-power and security goals better.

This table is Chapter 3's "sensor selection" logic applied one level up, to the board rather than the sensor: match the project's actual constraint (power, AI compute, display, industrial security) to the specific variant built for it, rather than defaulting to whichever board is most familiar.

The applications list — smart home, home automation, smart agriculture, weather monitoring, smart parking, wearables, robotics, smart energy meters, healthcare devices, industrial IoT — is really just Chapter 1's industry verticals, revisited from the hardware side: every one of those verticals needs a board that's cheap, low-power, and wireless-ready, which is exactly the ESP32's design brief.

ARM architecture

ARM (Advanced RISC Machines) is a semiconductor company that designs processor architectures, not chips themselves — ARM licenses its designs to companies like Espressif, Qualcomm, and Apple, who then manufacture actual silicon around them. ARM processors are built on RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) principles: a simplified instruction set that trades away some of the flexibility of a larger instruction set for higher performance per watt and simpler, faster execution.

Key features: 32-bit and 64-bit RISC designs, low power consumption for battery-operated devices, high performance per watt, fast instruction execution, a compact instruction set, real-time processing support, scalability from tiny microcontrollers to high-end processors, integrated security (TrustZone, in many devices), and a large software/development ecosystem. That scalability claim is the important one — it's the reason the same underlying architecture shows up in a $2 sensor chip and a $1000 smartphone.

Three ARM families, three different jobs

FamilyDesigned forExamplesUsed in
Cortex-M (M0/M3/M4/M7)Microcontrollers — low power, real-time operationIoT devices, robotics, medical devices, automotive electronicsThe ESP32's own processor lineage sits in this space
Cortex-R (R5/R52)Real-time systems — high reliability, deterministic performanceAutomotive systems, industrial control, SSD controllers, aerospaceWhere "always respond within X milliseconds, guaranteed" matters more than raw speed
Cortex-A (A53/A72/A78)Application processors — runs full operating systemsSmartphones, tablets, Raspberry Pi, smart TVs, networking devicesAnything running Linux, Android, or Windows

ARM's key highlights across all three families: RISC-based, low power consumption, high performance and efficiency, and scalability from small MCUs to high-end processors. The rest of this section derives why Cortex-M and Cortex-A end up looking so different internally, even though both trace back to the same RISC philosophy.

Cortex-M, up close

Everything on this diagram is built around one goal: respond to the outside world instantly and predictably, using as little power as possible. Read it as a signal's path rather than a list of boxes:

BlockRole
CPU Core32-bit RISC core running Thumb/Thumb-2 instructions, on a Harvard architecture (separate instruction and data pathways, so both can be fetched at once)
NVIC (Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller)Efficiently manages and prioritizes interrupts, with fast response — this is the piece that lets a button press or sensor threshold instantly divert the CPU's attention
SysTick TimerA 24-bit down-counter generating periodic interrupts, used for OS ticks and time delays
System Bus (AHB-Lite)The high-speed internal bus connecting every module together
GPIO / Timers / ADC-DAC / UART / SPI / I²CThe same peripheral set introduced for the ESP32 above — digital I/O, PWM/counting, analog conversion, and the three serial communication standards
MemoryFlash/ROM for code, SRAM for variables and runtime data, plus system memory for special-function and configuration registers
The NVIC is the piece that makes "real-time" actually true A plain desktop CPU checks for new input more or less whenever the operating system gets around to it. The NVIC exists so a Cortex-M chip can interrupt whatever it's doing the instant a specific event occurs — a GPIO pin changing state, a timer expiring — and jump straight to the code that handles it, with prioritization so a critical event (an emergency stop button) can pre-empt a less urgent one (a routine sensor poll). This hardware feature is what turns "real-time response," Chapter 2's architectural driver, from a design goal into something the chip can actually guarantee.

Overall benefits: low power and high efficiency, fast interrupt handling, real-time performance, scalability from small MCUs to high-end embedded systems, and wide use across embedded and IoT applications.

Cortex-A, up close

Compare this to the Cortex-M diagram above, block by block, and the design philosophy flips: Cortex-A is built to run full operating systems and juggle many programs at once, not to react to one sensor event as fast as possible.

BlockRole
CPU Core (ARMv8-A/v9-A)32-bit/64-bit RISC with out-of-order execution, a superscalar pipeline, a NEON SIMD engine, a floating-point unit, and its own L1 instruction/data cache
GIC (Generic Interrupt Controller)Manages interrupts across potentially many CPU cores
MMU (Memory Management Unit)Virtual memory support, memory protection, address translation — the thing that lets multiple programs each believe they have their own private memory space, which is required to run a real OS
L2 CacheShared cache reducing memory latency across cores
AMBA/AXI InterconnectHigh-speed, high-bandwidth bus connecting every subsystem
Multimedia blockGPU, 2D/3D engine, display controller, camera interface, video codec, audio DSP
Security blockTrustZone, secure boot, crypto engine, secure key storage
Debug & TraceCoreSight debug, JTAG/SWD, performance monitoring
The MMU is the single biggest tell Cortex-M has no MMU; Cortex-A always does. An MMU is what makes it possible to run Linux or Android — a real OS needs to give each running app the illusion of its own isolated memory, and to swap data to disk when RAM runs out. A microcontroller running one dedicated program (Chapter 5's Arduino setup()/loop()) has no such need: there's only ever one program, so there's nothing to isolate it from. This single missing block explains most of the rest of the difference between the two families.

Benefits: high performance for complex applications, runs advanced operating systems, supports high-resolution displays and multimedia, enhanced security and memory protection, scalable from single-core to multi-core, and used across smartphones, tablets, TVs, set-top boxes, Raspberry Pi, networking devices, and more.

Cortex-M vs. Cortex-A, side by side

ARM Cortex-M (MCU)ARM Cortex-A (MPU)
Operating systemRTOS (or no OS at all)Linux / Android
Power consumptionLowHigh
PerformanceMediumVery high
CacheSmallLarge
MMUNoYes
Wi-Fi / BluetoothExternal (added separately)External (added separately)
Best forLow power, real-time control, small & cost-effective, simple embedded tasksHigh performance, multimedia & graphics, large memory support, complex applications
Example chipsSTM32, NXP LPC, Nordic nRF52, Texas Instruments TivaQualcomm Snapdragon, Samsung Exynos, Raspberry Pi, Apple A-series
ApplicationsEmbedded systems, industrial, IoT, sensorsSmartphones, tablets, Raspberry Pi, smart TVs
Bringing this back to Chapter 3's board comparison: the Arduino Uno and ESP32 run Cortex-M-class (or comparable AVR/Xtensa) designs — no OS, one program, instant response. The Raspberry Pi runs a Cortex-A chip, because it needs to boot Linux and juggle a camera feed, a network stack, and your Python script all at once. Neither design is "better" in the abstract — Cortex-M wins wherever Chapter 2's power-and-cost driver dominates, Cortex-A wins wherever raw compute and multitasking dominate. This is the same one-size-doesn't-fit-all lesson as Chapter 2's architecture models and Chapter 1's connectivity table, now at the level of the chip itself.
